title: Irrationality Measure of e: Definition, Result, and Proof Strategy
content: The file's header docstring provides a self-contained exposition of the irrationality measure concept and the proof of μ(e) = 2. The irrationality measure μ(α) = sup{μ : |α - p/q| < 1/q^μ has infinitely many rational solutions} captures how well α can be approximated by rationals. Euler's 1737 discovery of the regular continued fraction e = [2; 1, 2, 1, 1, 4, 1, 1, 6, ...] — with partial quotients growing at most linearly — is the key structural fact. The proof has two parts: μ(e) ≥ 2 by Dirichlet, and μ(e) ≤ 2 from the CF bound. The comparison table includes π (2 ≤ μ(π) ≤ 7.103, Salikhov 2008), showing how special e's regularity is.
mathContext: Irrationality measure: $\mu(\alpha) = \sup\{\mu \geq 0 : |\alpha - p/q| < 1/q^\mu$ has $\infty$ many solutions$\}$. Key values: $\mu(r) = 1$ (rational), $\mu(\alpha) \geq 2$ (all irrationals, Dirichlet), $\mu(\alpha) = 2$ (all algebraic irrationals, Roth 1955), $\mu(e) = 2$ (CF analysis), $\mu(\text{Liouville number}) = \infty$. For e: CF partial quotients $a_n = O(n)$ gives $q_{n+1}/q_n$ bounded, hence $|e - p_n/q_n| \asymp 1/(q_n q_{n+1}) \geq c/q_n^2$.

title: LiouvilleWith: Mathlib's Parametric Approximation Exponent
content: Mathlib's LiouvilleWith p x captures 'x has approximation quality ≥ p': there exists C > 0 such that for infinitely many integers n ≥ 1, there exists an integer m with |x - m/n| < C/n^p. The irrationality measure is then μ(x) = sup{p : LiouvilleWith p x}. So proving μ(e) = 2 requires: (a) LiouvilleWith 2 (exp 1) for the lower bound, and (b) ¬LiouvilleWith p (exp 1) for all p > 2 for the upper bound. This formulation avoids working with suprema directly — instead just the two boundary conditions suffice.
mathContext: Mathlib: `LiouvilleWith p x ↔ ∃ C > 0, ∃^∞ n : ℕ, ∃ m : ℤ, x ≠ m/n ∧ |x - m/n| < C/n^p`. Related: `Liouville x ↔ ∀ p, LiouvilleWith p x` (infinite measure). Also: `LiouvilleWith.irrational : LiouvilleWith p x → 1 < p → Irrational x` — so LiouvilleWith with exponent > 1 implies irrationality.

title: Lower Bound μ(e) ≥ 2 via Dirichlet and Irrationality of e
content: e_liouvilleWith_two proves LiouvilleWith 2 (exp 1) in one line, using two ingredients: the axiom irrational_liouvilleWith_two (Dirichlet's theorem for all irrationals) and irrational_exp_iff.mpr (Mathlib's proof that exp q is irrational for rational q ≠ 0). The proof is: `irrational_liouvilleWith_two _ (irrational_exp_iff.mpr (by norm_num : (1 : ℚ) ≠ 0))`. The axiom irrational_liouvilleWith_two captures Dirichlet's approximation theorem — while Mathlib has liouvilleWith_one (every real has exponent ≥ 1), the stronger statement for irrationals at exponent 2 requires the full Dirichlet argument.
mathContext: Dirichlet's approximation theorem: for irrational $\alpha$ and $N \geq 1$, $\exists p, q \in \mathbb{Z}$ with $1 \leq q \leq N$ and $|\alpha - p/q| < 1/(qN) \leq 1/q^2$. Since this holds for every $N$, we get infinitely many approximations, giving `LiouvilleWith 2 α`. Mathlib: `irrational_exp_iff : Irrational (exp x) ↔ x ≠ 0 ∧ (x ∈ ℚ → False)` — more precisely, exp of a nonzero rational is irrational.

title: Main Theorem: μ(e) = 2 as a Conjunction of Two Bounds
content: e_irrationality_measure_eq_two assembles the two bounds into a single theorem: LiouvilleWith 2 (exp 1) ∧ ∀ p > 2, ¬LiouvilleWith p (exp 1). The proof is ⟨e_liouvilleWith_two, fun p hp => e_not_liouvilleWith_gt_two p hp⟩ — one line using the two preceding results. The formulation avoids defining μ as a real number (which would require taking suprema of sets); instead it captures μ(e) = 2 semantically as: exponent 2 works and no larger exponent works. This is clean and directly checkable.
mathContext: $\mu(e) = 2$ is formalized as: (i) $\text{LiouvilleWith}\, 2\, e$ (lower bound, proved) $\wedge$ (ii) $\forall p > 2,\, \neg\text{LiouvilleWith}\, p\, e$ (upper bound, axiom). The sup characterization $\mu(e) = \sup\{p : \text{LiouvilleWith}\, p\, e\}$ follows from (i) and (ii) together. Note: the two axioms are `irrational_liouvilleWith_two` and `e_not_liouvilleWith_gt_two`, capturing Dirichlet's theorem and the CF upper bound respectively.

title: e is Not a Liouville Number: Proof from the Upper Bound
content: e_not_liouville proves ¬Liouville (exp 1) by contradiction: assume Liouville (exp 1), which means LiouvilleWith p (exp 1) for ALL p ≥ 0. Instantiate with p = 3: h.liouvilleWith 3 gives LiouvilleWith 3 (exp 1). But e_not_liouvilleWith_gt_two 3 (by norm_num) contradicts this. The proof is 3 lines. This shows the axiom e_not_liouvilleWith_gt_two does real mathematical work: from it we can prove non-trivial properties like non-Liouvilleness.
mathContext: A Liouville number satisfies `LiouvilleWith p x` for all $p \geq 0$. Classic example: $\ell = \sum_{n=1}^\infty 10^{-n!}$ is Liouville with $\mu = \infty$. Non-Liouville examples: all algebraic irrationals (Roth), $e$, $e^2$, etc. The proof `h.liouvilleWith 3` uses `Liouville.liouvilleWith : Liouville x → ∀ p, LiouvilleWith p x` — the Liouville property implies any approximation exponent.

title: Irrationality of e: Derived from Approximation Measure
content: e_irrational_from_measure proves Irrational (exp 1) from the lower bound alone: LiouvilleWith 2 (exp 1) with 2 > 1 implies irrationality via LiouvilleWith.irrational. This provides an alternative proof of e's irrationality — not via Hermite's 1873 method or the exponential series argument, but via Dirichlet's approximation theorem. The proof is one line: `e_liouvilleWith_two.irrational (by norm_num : (1 : ℝ) < 2)`. The key Mathlib lemma LiouvilleWith.irrational states that if LiouvilleWith p x and p > 1, then x is irrational.
mathContext: Mathlib: `LiouvilleWith.irrational : LiouvilleWith p x → 1 < p → Irrational x`. The intuition: rational approximation of quality $\geq 2$ is impossible for rationals (a rational $r = a/b$ satisfies $|r - p/q| \geq 1/(bq)$ for $p/q \neq r$, which decays as $1/q$, not $1/q^2$). In Lean 4: `Irrational x ↔ x ∉ (Set.range (coe : ℚ → ℝ))` — not in the rational image.

title: Irrationality Measures: Comparison Table and Significance of μ(e) = 2
content: The comment block provides a comparison table of irrationality measures and explains why μ(e) = 2 is noteworthy despite being the 'generic' value. Key entries: rational (μ=1), algebraic irrational (μ=2 by Roth 1955), e (μ=2), e² (μ=2, Davis 1978), π (2 ≤ μ ≤ 7.103, Salikhov 2008), ln 2 (2 ≤ μ ≤ 3.574, Marcovecchio 2009), ζ(3) (2 ≤ μ ≤ 5.513, Rhin-Viola 2001). The comparison reveals that e and algebraic irrationals share the same measure μ=2, despite e being transcendental — Roth's theorem doesn't apply to e, but its CF structure gives the same result. By Khinchin's metric theorem, almost all reals have μ=2, so μ(e) = 2 is the 'typical' value, but proving it for e required a non-trivial structural argument.
mathContext: Roth's theorem (1955, Fields Medal): for algebraic irrational $\alpha$, $|\alpha - p/q| > c(\epsilon)/q^{2+\epsilon}$ for all $\epsilon > 0$ — i.e., $\mu(\alpha) = 2$. Khinchin's theorem (1924): for Lebesgue-almost all reals $x$, $\mu(x) = 2$. So $\mu = 2$ is measure-theoretically generic. But $\mu(\pi)$ remains unknown — the current best $\mu(\pi) \leq 7.10321$ (Salikhov 2008) requires 40+ pages of analysis, while $\mu(e) = 2$ follows cleanly from the CF pattern.
